script.opening: "Hi, um — I need the morning-after pill please. We didn't use anything and I really don't want to be pregnant. Can I just get it sorted today, like at the chemist or whatever? I'd rather not go through a load of questions if that's okay, it's a bit embarrassing. How quickly can I get it?"

facts.text: If asked: Saturday night — "about three days ago, so like 72 hours". Only once since your last period. No condom.
If asked: regular, every 28 days. Last period started about two weeks ago, so you are mid-cycle. You have not had any other unprotected sex this cycle.

Not on any contraception. Never used emergency contraception before. No medical problems, no regular medicines, no allergies. You are not on anything for epilepsy or HIV, and do not take any herbal remedies.
No discharge, no pain, no bleeding. Never had an STI test.
Aimee, 16, in Year 12 at college. Lives with mum and stepdad. Mum does not know you are sexually active.

facts.topic: The boyfriend — only if asked gently and without judgement
facts.text: His name is Ryan. "He's 25. We met on Instagram about two months ago." He picks you up from college in his car. He bought you a new phone. He says you should keep it quiet "because people wouldn't understand". If asked whether he ever pressures you: "Not really... he gets annoyed if I don't reply straight away." He did not want to use a condom.

He has asked you to come to a party at his friend's flat this weekend and stay over; you feel a bit uneasy about it but "it's probably fine". Say this only if the doctor has built trust and asks whether you feel safe.

Embarrassed, in a hurry, a bit defensive. If questions about the boyfriend feel like a telling-off, clam up: "Can I just get the pill?" If the doctor first reassures you that you WILL get emergency contraception today and explains why they ask, answer more openly. You are not keen on a coil ("that sounds painful") but will listen. You want to keep it from your mum; if the doctor explains when they might need to share information, you are anxious but will ask "Would you tell me first?"

ice.ideas: "I just need the morning-after pill and it'll be fine."
ice.concerns: "I really can't be pregnant." Underneath: you half-know other people would be worried about Ryan, and you do not want anyone to find out.
ice.expectations: "Just sort it today, no questions." You will answer questions if you feel they are not judging you and you are sure you will still get the pill.

cues: "I'd rather not go through a load of questions." — say in the opening.
"He's a bit older." — say vaguely if asked about your partner; give his age only if asked directly.
"He says people wouldn't understand." — say if the relationship is explored.

checkpoints.text: Provides EMERGENCY CONTRACEPTION promptly without unnecessary barriers, AND advises on the most effective method (CoSRH 2017, amended 2023): the COPPER IUD is the most effective EC (offer/recommend, effective up to 5 days; if a fitting is being arranged, give oral EC now in case it cannot happen), with oral options ulipristal acetate (up to 120 h, preferred over levonorgestrel at ~72 h/mid-cycle) and levonorgestrel — chosen by timing/cycle and patient preference

Knows that at 16 she is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and can consent to her own treatment (Family Law Reform Act 1969 s8) — Fraser criteria apply to under-16s — and checks her understanding and best interests appropriately, while not creating barriers to a time-sensitive treatment she is entitled to

Screens for SAFEGUARDING/CSE: gently explores the relationship (partner age 25, met online), coercion/control, capacity to consent, and other exploitation indicators — recognising the significant age gap and online pattern as red flags requiring sensitive assessment and possible safeguarding action per local pathways (a structured tool such as the BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma, 2014; discuss with the practice safeguarding lead)

Addresses ONGOING contraception (so she’s not back in the same position) and STI risk (testing/screening), and advises a pregnancy test 3 weeks after the unprotected sex (CoSRH 2017), or sooner if her period is late or unusual

Knows the practical points: ulipristal vs levonorgestrel interaction (don’t mix; quick-starting hormonal contraception differs after ulipristal), to repeat the dose if vomiting occurs within 3 hours (CoSRH), and that EC does not protect for the rest of the cycle
Meets her need promptly and non-judgementally so she stays engaged, while gently raising the safeguarding questions in a way that doesn’t feel like interrogation or alienate her

Balances her autonomy and confidentiality with the duty to safeguard — being honest about limits if a serious safeguarding concern requires sharing information, ideally with her involvement (GMC 0–18 years guidance)

Safety-nets and follows up: pregnancy test 3 weeks after the unprotected sex (CoSRH 2017) — sooner if her period is more than 7 days late or lighter than usual, STI screen and ongoing-contraception plan, safeguarding referral/discussion as indicated, sources of support, and a route back — prompt access AND safeguarding both delivered

worked.txt: "Of course — and well done for sorting this quickly, that’s the sensible thing. I can absolutely help you get emergency contraception today. Let me ask just a few quick things so I give you the option that works best for you, not to make it awkward — is that okay?"

"When exactly was the unprotected sex? … About three days ago, and roughly mid-cycle. That matters: there’s a tablet called ellaOne that works better than the standard morning-after pill at this point, and there’s also a small coil that’s actually the most effective option of all and can go in up to five days after — it also then keeps protecting you. I’ll talk you through both so you can choose."

"Can I ask a bit about your partner, just so I’m looking after you properly? … He’s 25, and you met online. Okay. I’m not judging you at all — I ask because when there’s a bigger age gap, I just want to make sure you feel completely in control and that everything’s happening because YOU want it to. How did things start between you?"

"You’ve handled this really maturely. The reason I gently ask is part of my job is making sure no one’s taking advantage or pressuring you — and if anything ever didn’t feel okay, I’d help, not judge. Most of what you tell me stays private; the only time I’d need to involve anyone else is if I were worried about your safety, and I’d talk to you first."

"Two more useful things: shall we sort some regular contraception so you’re not back here stressed again — there are options that are very reliable and easy. And because no condom was used, it’s worth a quick check for infections too, all confidential. None of that has to be a big deal."

"So — I’ll get you the emergency contraception today and explain the choices. If you’re sick within 3 hours of the tablet, ring back as you’ll need another. Do a pregnancy test three weeks after the unprotected sex — or sooner if your period’s more than a week late or seems different. And you can come back to me about ANYTHING — the relationship, contraception, infections, anything at all. You’re not in trouble and you’re not on your own."

f.learning: An emergency-contraception request from a 16-year-old must deliver TWO things at once: prompt, barrier-free access to effective EC, AND a sensitive safeguarding assessment. On method, advise by timing/cycle — the COPPER IUD is the most effective EC (up to 5 days, and provides ongoing contraception), ulipristal acetate is preferred over levonorgestrel at ~72 h/mid-cycle (effective up to 120 h), and levonorgestrel up to 72 h; mind the practical points (CoSRH 2017, amended 2023: don’t mix ulipristal and levonorgestrel, repeat if vomiting within 3 hours, EC doesn’t cover the rest of the cycle, quick-start ongoing contraception, pregnancy test 3 weeks after the unprotected sex). At 16 she is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005; Fraser criteria are for under-16s) — check understanding without obstructing a time-sensitive treatment she is entitled to. The examinable core is the SAFEGUARDING red flag — a 25-year-old partner met online — which, despite 16 being the age of consent, raises CSE/exploitation and coercion concerns to be explored gently and acted on per local pathways, balancing her autonomy/confidentiality with the duty to safeguard (honest about limits, ideally involving her). Address ongoing contraception and STI screening, and meet her need non-judgementally so she stays engaged. If clarified: the UPSI was ~72 hours ago, mid-cycle (higher conception risk). Method matters (CoSRH — formerly FSRH — Emergency contraception guideline, 2017, amended 2023): the COPPER IUD is the most effective EC (up to 120 hours after the first UPSI in the cycle, or up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation) and should be offered/recommended; oral options are ulipristal acetate (ellaOne, up to 120 h, more effective than levonorgestrel, especially mid-cycle/later) and levonorgestrel (up to 72 h). At ~72 h mid-cycle, ulipristal or the copper IUD are preferable to levonorgestrel.

knowledge.guideline: CoSRH (formerly FSRH) Emergency contraception guideline (2017, amended April 2026) · GMC 0–18 years guidance · Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023) · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · Sexual Offences Act 2003
knowledge.summary: Aimee needs effective emergency contraception today: the copper IUD first, or ulipristal if she prefers a tablet. A 25-year-old partner she met online is a safeguarding cue that needs a gentle, honest exploration — without putting her off care.

points.t: CoSRH 2017: the copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception. It can be fitted up to 120 hours after the first unprotected sex in the cycle, or up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation. It then gives ongoing contraception.

Ulipristal acetate 30 mg works up to 120 hours after unprotected sex; levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is licensed up to 72 hours (3 mg if BMI over 26 or weight over 70 kg). At around 72 hours, mid-cycle, ulipristal is the better tablet. Oral EC should be given now if an IUD fitting is being arranged, in case it cannot happen.

Repeat the dose if she vomits within 3 hours. After ulipristal, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception, using condoms or avoiding sex meanwhile. EC does not protect against later sex in the same cycle. Pregnancy test 3 weeks after the unprotected sex (CoSRH 2017).

At 16 she is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and can consent to her own treatment; Fraser criteria apply to under-16s. She is still a child for safeguarding purposes until 18 (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023).

16 is the age of consent, but a large age gap and meeting online are recognised risk indicators for exploitation. Use a structured approach (BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs, 2014): how they met, pressure, gifts, secrecy, alcohol or drugs, isolation. Sex with a 16- or 17-year-old is an offence if the adult is in a position of trust (Sexual Offences Act 2003).

GMC 0–18 years: keep her information confidential unless there is a risk of serious harm, in which case share it with the appropriate agency, ideally with her knowledge. Discuss concerns with the practice safeguarding lead.

dg.d: Met the request immediately and explained why a few questions were needed.
Explored the relationship and her own sense that others would worry about it, without pressing.
Timing of unprotected sex, cycle, other exposures, medicines; STI testing and pregnancy test planned.
Pregnancy risk by timing and cycle; exploitation versus a consensual relationship; STI risk.
Safeguarding indicators screened with a structured approach; plan to discuss with the safeguarding lead if concerns persist.
Clear statement of what the options are and why ulipristal or copper IUD suit her timing.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Copper IUD offered first; ulipristal prescribed today by her choice; ongoing contraception and STI screen booked.
Capacity at 16 respected; confidentiality and its limits explained honestly; safeguarding lead discussion documented.
Vomiting rule, 5-day wait before hormones, condoms, pregnancy test at 3 weeks, Childline, face-to-face follow-up booked.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “he’s really nice though”, “mostly” and “I don’t want to get him in trouble” and explored them.
Idea (a quick morning-after pill); concern (embarrassment, scrutiny of the relationship); expectation (no questions).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I really can't be pregnant." Underneath: you half-know other people would be worried about Ryan, and you do not want anyone to find out — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I check who I’m speaking to and your date of birth? … Thanks, Aimee. Are you somewhere you can talk without being overheard?
model.why: Confirms identity and privacy before a sensitive call

model.text: Yeah, it’s fine. I need the morning-after pill. We didn’t use anything. Can I just get it today? I’d rather not have loads of questions, it’s embarrassing.
You’ve done exactly the right thing ringing quickly, and yes, we can sort this today. I’ll keep the questions to the ones that help me give you the option that works best. Is that okay?
model.why: Meets her need immediately and explains why questions matter

model.text: Okay.
When did you have sex without protection — as close as you can remember?
model.why: Establishes timing, which drives the method

model.text: Three days ago. At night.
And when did your last period start? Has there been any other unprotected sex since then?
About two weeks before that. No, just the once.
Thanks. Are you on any medicines, including anything from a shop, and have you any health problems I should know about?
No, nothing.

That timing matters. You’re around three days on, and mid-cycle. The most effective option is a small copper coil — it can go in up to five days after, and then keeps protecting you for years. The other option is a tablet called ulipristal, which works better than the standard morning-after pill at this point.
model.why: Offers the copper IUD first and the right oral option

model.text: A coil? That sounds a lot. I’d rather just have a tablet.
That’s completely your choice. I’ll prescribe ulipristal today. If you change your mind about the coil, it needs to go in within the next two days, and I can help arrange that.
model.why: Respects her choice and keeps the more effective option open

model.text: Okay. Tablet.
Can I ask a bit about your partner? I ask everyone your age — it’s not about judging you, it’s about making sure you’re okay. How old is he, and how did you meet?
model.why: Normalises the question before asking it

model.text: (Pause.) He’s 25. We met online. He’s really nice though.
Thank you for being honest. How are things between you — do you feel you’re the one deciding what happens, including about sex?
model.why: Explores consent and control without accusation

model.text: Yeah… mostly. I don’t know. I know people would say he’s too old.
It sounds like there’s a bit you’re unsure about, and that’s okay to say. Has he ever asked you to keep things secret, given you things, or asked you to do things you didn’t want to?
Not really. I don’t want to get him in trouble.

I hear that. What we talk about stays between us. The only time I’d need to share anything is if I was worried you might be at risk of serious harm — and if that happened, I’d talk to you first. Would you be willing to come in and see me, or the sexual health clinic, this week so we can talk a bit more?
model.why: Honest about confidentiality limits and keeps her engaged

model.text: Maybe. If it’s just you.
That’s fine. When you come in, we can also sort regular contraception, and a check for infections, because no condom was used. Both are quick and confidential.
model.why: Plans ongoing contraception and STI testing

model.text: Okay, that makes sense.

A few important things about the tablet. If you’re sick within three hours, ring back — you’ll need another. It doesn’t protect you for the rest of this month, so use condoms. And don’t start any hormonal contraception for five days after taking it, because it can stop the tablet working.
Do a pregnancy test three weeks after the sex, even if you have a bleed. And if you ever feel unsafe or pressured, you can ring me or Childline any time. Can you tell me what you’re going to do?
model.why: Pregnancy test timing, support options, teach-back

model.text: Get the tablet today, ring if I’m sick, condoms, pregnancy test in three weeks, come in this week.
Perfect. I’ll send the prescription now and book you in with me this week. You’ve handled this really sensibly.
Thanks. That was less awful than I thought.

social.t: A 25-year-old partner met online, and her sense that others would disapprove. These are cues to explore, not proof of harm.
Young people often give up if care is hard to reach. Make the prescription and follow-up simple and quick.

legal.t: At 16 she is presumed to have capacity and can consent to treatment (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Fraser criteria are for under-16s.
The age of consent is 16. Sexual activity with a 16- or 17-year-old is an offence if the adult is in a position of trust.
She is a child for safeguarding purposes until 18 (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023). Share information if there is a risk of serious harm.

professional.t: Provide confidential sexual health care to young people, and share information when needed to protect them, ideally with their knowledge.
Discuss and document concerns with the practice safeguarding lead; use a structured tool such as Spotting the Signs (BASHH and Brook, 2014).

community.t: Local young people’s sexual health service; Brook; Childline for confidential support.

redFlags: Large age gap, met online, secrecy — exploitation indicators
Pressure, gifts, alcohol or drugs, being isolated from friends or family
Earlier unprotected sex this cycle — possible existing pregnancy
psychosocial: Senses others would worry about the age gap
Worried about getting the partner into trouble
ice: Idea: she just needs the morning-after pill
Concern: embarrassment; questions about the relationship

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear about the pregnancy risk: “Three days after sex around the middle of your cycle is a time when pregnancy is possible, so the method matters.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Emergency contraception works by delaying the egg being released. The coil works even if it already has been. That’s why it’s the most effective, and why timing matters for the tablets.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you wanted this quick and without questions. You’ll have it today — and I asked about your partner because I ask everyone, and I want to know you’re okay.”
management.psychosocial: Keep her engaged: face-to-face follow-up with the same doctor; honest confidentiality; support options she can use herself.
sharedPlan: Copper IUD offered (within 120 hours); ulipristal 30 mg prescribed today by her choice
Ongoing contraception after the 5-day wait; condoms meanwhile; STI testing
Safeguarding discussion with the practice lead; follow-up this week
safetyNet: Vomits within 3 hours — ring back for another dose
Pregnancy test 3 weeks after the sex; Childline or the surgery if she feels unsafe

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you can deliver time-sensitive care and safeguarding in the same ten minutes. Candidates fail by doing only one of them, or by doing the safeguarding so bluntly that she hangs up.

items.fail: Sending levonorgestrel without thinking about timing.
items.why: At about 72 hours, mid-cycle, levonorgestrel is at the edge of its licence and less effective. CoSRH 2017 puts the copper IUD first.
items.fix: Offer the IUD first, ulipristal as the tablet, and explain why.

items.why: “Does not identify safeguarding concerns.” The 25-year-old met online is the examinable core.
items.fix: Ask everyone her age: partner’s age, how they met, pressure, secrecy, gifts.

items.fail: Delaying EC until the safeguarding picture is clear.
items.why: EC is time-critical and she is entitled to it. Safeguarding runs alongside treatment, not before it.
items.fix: Prescribe today, then explore and plan follow-up.

items.why: It misstates GMC guidance and breaks trust if you later need to share.
items.fix: Explain the limit honestly and promise to talk to her first.

items.fail: Using a disapproving tone about the age gap.
items.why: She will defend him and disengage; examiners mark this as poor rapport.
items.fix: Curiosity, not judgement: “How are things between you?”

items.fail: Ending the call with a prescription and nothing else.
items.why: Misses ongoing contraception, STI testing, pregnancy test timing and safeguarding follow-up.
items.fix: Book face-to-face follow-up, give the counselling points and support options, and document the safeguarding discussion.

timeMap.d: Confirm she can talk privately, and say yes to helping today before any questions.
When was the unprotected sex, LMP, other exposures, medicines. That decides the method.
Copper IUD first, ulipristal as the tablet at 72 hours mid-cycle. Respect her choice.
Ask everyone: partner’s age, how they met, control, secrecy, gifts. Explain confidentiality and its limits honestly.
Contraception, STI screen, vomiting rule, 5-day wait, pregnancy test at 3 weeks, Childline, follow-up booked.

wordPics.fail: Either refuses or delays EC until safeguarding is resolved, or prescribes levonorgestrel without considering timing and never asks about the partner; interrogates her so she disengages; promises total secrecy.
wordPics.pass: Provides ulipristal promptly and mentions the copper IUD; asks the partner’s age and recognises a safeguarding concern; offers STI testing and contraception; gives a pregnancy test safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: offers the IUD first and keeps it open within the window; explores the relationship using specific indicators without accusation; explains confidentiality limits honestly; secures a face-to-face follow-up; plans a safeguarding lead discussion; accurate counselling (vomiting, 5-day wait, condoms, test at 3 weeks).

avoid.dont: "He’s 25 and you’re 16 — that’s not okay, is it?"
avoid.instead: "I ask everyone your age about their partner. How are things between you?"
avoid.why: Accusation makes her defend him and disengage; curiosity keeps her talking.

avoid.dont: "Don’t worry, everything you tell me is completely confidential."
avoid.instead: "What we talk about stays between us, unless I’m worried you’re at risk of serious harm — and then I’d talk to you first."
avoid.why: A promise you cannot keep breaks trust later and misstates the law.

avoid.dont: "I’ll send the standard morning-after pill to the pharmacy."
avoid.instead: "At three days, mid-cycle, the coil is the most effective, and ulipristal is the better tablet."
avoid.why: Method choice by timing is a core Tasks point.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: CoSRH (formerly FSRH) Emergency contraception guideline (2017, amended April 2026) · GMC 0–18 years guidance · Working Together to Safeguard Children (2023) · BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs proforma (2014) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 · Sexual Offences Act 2003
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Aimee needs effective emergency contraception today: the copper IUD first, or ulipristal if she prefers a tablet. A 25-year-old partner she met online is a safeguarding cue that needs a gentle, honest exploration — without putting her off care.

points.t: CoSRH 2017: the copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception. It can be fitted up to 120 hours after the first unprotected sex in the cycle, or up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation. It then gives ongoing contraception.

Ulipristal acetate 30 mg works up to 120 hours after unprotected sex; levonorgestrel 1.5 mg is licensed up to 72 hours (3 mg if BMI over 26 or weight over 70 kg). At around 72 hours, mid-cycle, ulipristal is the better tablet. Oral EC should be given now if an IUD fitting is being arranged, in case it cannot happen.

Repeat the dose if she vomits within 3 hours. After ulipristal, wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception, using condoms or avoiding sex meanwhile. EC does not protect against later sex in the same cycle. Pregnancy test 3 weeks after the unprotected sex (CoSRH 2017).

At 16 she is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and can consent to her own treatment; Fraser criteria apply to under-16s. She is still a child for safeguarding purposes until 18 (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023).

16 is the age of consent, but a large age gap and meeting online are recognised risk indicators for exploitation. Use a structured approach (BASHH and Brook Spotting the Signs, 2014): how they met, pressure, gifts, secrecy, alcohol or drugs, isolation. Sex with a 16- or 17-year-old is an offence if the adult is in a position of trust (Sexual Offences Act 2003).

GMC 0–18 years: keep her information confidential unless there is a risk of serious harm, in which case share it with the appropriate agency, ideally with her knowledge. Discuss concerns with the practice safeguarding lead.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Met the request immediately and explained why a few questions were needed.
Explored the relationship and her own sense that others would worry about it, without pressing.
Picked up “he’s really nice though”, “mostly” and “I don’t want to get him in trouble” and explored them.
Idea (a quick morning-after pill); concern (embarrassment, scrutiny of the relationship); expectation (no questions).
Timing of unprotected sex, cycle, other exposures, medicines; STI testing and pregnancy test planned.
Pregnancy risk by timing and cycle; exploitation versus a consensual relationship; STI risk.
Safeguarding indicators screened with a structured approach; plan to discuss with the safeguarding lead if concerns persist.
Clear statement of what the options are and why ulipristal or copper IUD suit her timing.
Copper IUD offered first; ulipristal prescribed today by her choice; ongoing contraception and STI screen booked.
Capacity at 16 respected; confidentiality and its limits explained honestly; safeguarding lead discussion documented.
Vomiting rule, 5-day wait before hormones, condoms, pregnancy test at 3 weeks, Childline, face-to-face follow-up booked.

social.t: A 25-year-old partner met online, and her sense that others would disapprove. These are cues to explore, not proof of harm.
Young people often give up if care is hard to reach. Make the prescription and follow-up simple and quick.

legal.t: At 16 she is presumed to have capacity and can consent to treatment (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Fraser criteria are for under-16s.
The age of consent is 16. Sexual activity with a 16- or 17-year-old is an offence if the adult is in a position of trust.
She is a child for safeguarding purposes until 18 (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023). Share information if there is a risk of serious harm.

professional.t: Provide confidential sexual health care to young people, and share information when needed to protect them, ideally with their knowledge.
Discuss and document concerns with the practice safeguarding lead; use a structured tool such as Spotting the Signs (BASHH and Brook, 2014).

community.t: Local young people’s sexual health service; Brook; Childline for confidential support.

redFlags: Large age gap, met online, secrecy — exploitation indicators
Pressure, gifts, alcohol or drugs, being isolated from friends or family
Earlier unprotected sex this cycle — possible existing pregnancy
psychosocial: Senses others would worry about the age gap
Worried about getting the partner into trouble
ice: Idea: she just needs the morning-after pill
Concern: embarrassment; questions about the relationship

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear about the pregnancy risk: “Three days after sex around the middle of your cycle is a time when pregnancy is possible, so the method matters.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Emergency contraception works by delaying the egg being released. The coil works even if it already has been. That’s why it’s the most effective, and why timing matters for the tablets.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you wanted this quick and without questions. You’ll have it today — and I asked about your partner because I ask everyone, and I want to know you’re okay.”
management.psychosocial: Keep her engaged: face-to-face follow-up with the same doctor; honest confidentiality; support options she can use herself.
sharedPlan: Copper IUD offered (within 120 hours); ulipristal 30 mg prescribed today by her choice
Ongoing contraception after the 5-day wait; condoms meanwhile; STI testing
Safeguarding discussion with the practice lead; follow-up this week
safetyNet: Vomits within 3 hours — ring back for another dose
Pregnancy test 3 weeks after the sex; Childline or the surgery if she feels unsafe

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you can deliver time-sensitive care and safeguarding in the same ten minutes. Candidates fail by doing only one of them, or by doing the safeguarding so bluntly that she hangs up.

items.fail: Sending levonorgestrel without thinking about timing.
items.why: At about 72 hours, mid-cycle, levonorgestrel is at the edge of its licence and less effective. CoSRH 2017 puts the copper IUD first.
items.fix: Offer the IUD first, ulipristal as the tablet, and explain why.

items.why: “Does not identify safeguarding concerns.” The 25-year-old met online is the examinable core.
items.fix: Ask everyone her age: partner’s age, how they met, pressure, secrecy, gifts.

items.fail: Delaying EC until the safeguarding picture is clear.
items.why: EC is time-critical and she is entitled to it. Safeguarding runs alongside treatment, not before it.
items.fix: Prescribe today, then explore and plan follow-up.

items.why: It misstates GMC guidance and breaks trust if you later need to share.
items.fix: Explain the limit honestly and promise to talk to her first.

items.fail: Using a disapproving tone about the age gap.
items.why: She will defend him and disengage; examiners mark this as poor rapport.
items.fix: Curiosity, not judgement: “How are things between you?”

items.fail: Ending the call with a prescription and nothing else.
items.why: Misses ongoing contraception, STI testing, pregnancy test timing and safeguarding follow-up.
items.fix: Book face-to-face follow-up, give the counselling points and support options, and document the safeguarding discussion.
